newsitem.title: GREECE: European press urges West to help Albania.
newsitem.headline: European press urges West to help Albania.

text.p: European newspapers, incensed over emergency rule and censorship in Albania, urged Western governments to rush to prevent full-scale civil war in the tiny Balkan country.
"Democracy is staggering in Europe's poorest country. If it is not to be stifled altogether, free voices must be restored to print and the airwaves," the Times in London said in an editorial.

Albania's parliament declared a state of emergency on Sunday after weeks of violent protests in the southern region by thousands of investors who lost their savings in failed investment schemes. At least 20 people have died in the clashes.
Other British newspapers warned "mob rule looms" in Albania and urged the West to lend a helping hand.

"Whatever influence Western powers have on the situation has been exercised disgracefully. Once again in the Balkans, they have shown themselves to be morally at sea," said the Daily Telegraph in an editorial.

Albania's turmoil dominated the front pages of German newspapers. Die Welt carried the headline: "The war of a bankrupt government against its people. Albania urgently needs world's help to give those betrayed their money back."
Albanian President Sali Berisha has rejected opposition demands for a coalition government. He was elected unopposed by parliament to a second five-year term on March 3.

"The manner in which Berisha had himself re-elected as president...spoke volumes. It was a little play performed between the sliding doors of the presidential suite," said the Dutch daily Het Financieele Dagblad.
Blamed by the rioters for not warning them of the risks of the pyramid schemes, Berisha said he was determined to crush the unrest which has seen clashes between the army and insurgents in the south.
Austrian dailies devoted banner headlines to the crisis and criticised the European Union for its failure to intervene and prevent an escalation.

"Is Europe ready to intervene to stop the massacre, to provide humanitarian help and to force through new elections under international supervision? It does not look like it," the daily Die Presse said. "Europe remains silent."
On a similar theme, the Irish Times said divisions within the EU were preventing the 15-member bloc from acting fast to deal with yet another Balkan crisis on its doorstep.

"But the picture is a sorry one. It illustrates once again an overall ill-preparedness as well as a clear divergence among its member states, which repeats patterns of events as the Yugoslav crisis unfolded," the paper said.

The press in Albania's neighbours Italy and Greece, which have been flooded with illegal immigrants since the communist regime in Tirana collapsed in 1990, stressed concerns of another spillover and general unrest in the Balkans.
Italy's La Stampa said in a front page editorial Albania risked becoming "the Colombia of Europe...with dire consequences for public order and peace in our own country."

Greek newspapers, which have rushed an army of reporters to Albania, blamed the international community for its tolerance of Berisha and urged the EU to seek a political settlement and back it with aid.

"Europeans and Americans supported an undemocratic, authoritarian regime 'legitimised' by falsified elections, with opponents either persecuted or jailed," said the Eleftherotypia daily in its main editorial.
"The crisis can only be deflated by a government of national unity which will vote in the constitution that Albania lacks and lead to democracy," the paper said.
